title: Is Tithing Still Required Today? The Answer May Expose What Really Owns Your Heart
paragraphs: Is Tithing Still Required Today? The Answer May Expose What Really Owns Your Heart

Christians have argued over the ten percent for generations. But Jesus may be asking a far more uncomfortable question: not “How little must I give?” but “After the cross, how much of me still belongs to me?”
Imagine this.
Sunday morning. Worship has ended. The offering moment arrives.
You already know what is sitting in your bank account.
You know the electricity bill is coming.
You know what groceries cost now.
You know there is something your child needs.
You also remember the sermon somebody preached years ago: “If you don't give God ten percent, you're robbing Him.”
And suddenly something that was supposed to be worship feels like fear.
So your hand reaches for your wallet while your heart quietly asks a question you almost feel guilty for asking:
Does God really require Christians to tithe today?
Maybe you have been told that if you do not give exactly ten percent, you are disobedient.
Maybe you have heard Malachi 3 used like a spiritual invoice.
Maybe you were promised that if you tithed, God would make you financially prosperous.
Maybe you gave faithfully and then watched the medical bill arrive anyway.
The job still disappeared.
The business still struggled.
The prayer still seemed unanswered.
And somewhere inside you, a dangerous thought began forming:
Did God fail me?
Or perhaps you are standing on the opposite side.
You discovered that Christians live under the new covenant, concluded that tithing is “Old Testament,” and quietly turned Christian freedom into permission to give almost nothing.
That is why this question matters.
Because underneath the argument about ten percent is something much bigger.
Who owns your heart?
And Scripture's answer is more beautiful—and more demanding—than either legalism or selfishness.
The English word tithe simply means a tenth. In Hebrew, the important word is מַעֲשֵׂר — maʿaser, meaning “a tenth” or “tithe.”
Tithing appears before the Mosaic Law. Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils after battle in Genesis 14:18–20. Jacob later vowed to give God a tenth in Genesis 28:20–22.

But neither passage establishes a universal command requiring every believer in every age to surrender exactly ten percent of every form of income. They show that giving a tenth existed before Sinai, but description must not automatically be turned into command.
Then came Israel's covenant law.
And this is where modern conversations often become too simplistic.

Biblical Israel's tithing system was woven into the religious, agricultural, social, and covenant life of the nation. Numbers 18 describes support for the Levites. Deuteronomy 14 describes tithes connected with worship and also provision for Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. The Old Testament picture is therefore richer than the modern slogan, “God always requires ten percent of your paycheck.”
Then we arrive at the verse almost everyone knows.
Malachi 3:10 begins:
הָבִיאוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַמַּעֲשֵׂר אֶל־בֵּית הָאוֹצָר
Havi'u et-kol-hamma'aser el-beit ha'otzar...
“Bring the full tithe into the storehouse...”
That is genuinely what the Hebrew says. Ha-maʿaser is “the tithe,” and beit ha'otzar is the storehouse. Malachi speaks of food being present in God's house and of God's covenant blessing.
So Malachi 3 should not be erased.
But neither should it be ripped from its covenant setting and transformed into a Christian get-rich formula.

Malachi was confronting covenant unfaithfulness among God's people. This was not God handing the modern church a heavenly investment scheme in which ten percent deposited guarantees a larger financial withdrawal.
The God of Scripture is not a slot machine.
Giving is not a lever by which we force His hand.
And Jesus is not for sale.
Then someone will immediately say, “But Jesus Himself taught tithing.”
There is truth there that requires context.

In Matthew 23:23, Jesus rebuked scribes and Pharisees who carefully tithed even their herbs while neglecting “the weightier matters of the law”—justice, mercy, and faithfulness. He told them that they should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.
Jesus was not condemning their tithe.
He was condemning the grotesque contradiction of being meticulous about religious percentages while becoming spiritually blind to the heart of God's law.
Picture it.
A man carefully measures his mint.
His dill.
His cumin.
Everything mathematically correct.
Everything outwardly religious.
And standing in front of him is the Son of God saying, in effect:
You counted the leaves and missed the heart.
That should terrify religious people more than any argument about percentages.
Because it is possible to give ten percent and still worship money.
It is possible to tithe and remain greedy.
It is possible to put money into an offering while refusing mercy to somebody who desperately needs it.
It is possible to calculate exactly what “belongs to God” because, secretly, we want permission to call the remaining ninety percent ours.
Then Jesus goes to the cross.
A new covenant is inaugurated through His blood.
And when we turn to the New Testament instructions given to the churches, something striking happens.
The apostles repeatedly teach Christians to give.
Generously.
Sacrificially.
Intentionally.
Regularly.
Willingly.
According to their means.
For the poor.
For fellow believers.
For Gospel ministry.
For those laboring in the proclamation of the Gospel.
But the New Testament epistles do not plainly impose the Mosaic tithe as a universal ten-percent legal requirement upon Christians.
Paul's language in 2 Corinthians 9:7 is particularly important:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης· ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia, mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs; hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
The sense is:

Each person should give according to what he has determined in his heart, not from grief or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver. The Greek ἀνάγκη — anankē carries the idea of necessity, constraint, or compulsion, while ἱλαρός — hilaros describes the cheerful or willing character of the giver.
Read that again.
Not under compulsion.
That destroys one distortion of Christian giving.
But don't stop reading there.

Because the same chapter speaks about sowing generously, God's provision enabling good works, generosity toward others, meeting the needs of God's people, thanksgiving rising to God, and generosity resulting in God's glory.
That destroys the opposite distortion too.
Grace does not say:
“Great. I don't have to tithe, so I can keep everything.”
Grace asks:
“If Jesus gave Himself for me, how can generosity not transform me?”
This is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Under legalism, you ask:
What percentage do I have to surrender?
Under grace, you begin asking:
Lord, what have You entrusted to me, and how can I use it for Your glory?
Those are very different questions.
One searches for the minimum.
The other has seen Calvary.
Jesus did not purchase you with ten percent of His blood.
He gave Himself.

That does not mean Christians must donate everything they possess to a church or ministry. Scripture recognizes legitimate responsibilities toward family and personal needs. Paul strongly teaches responsibility for one's household in 1 Timothy 5:8. Biblical generosity is not financial recklessness, manipulation, neglect of dependents, or giving money you do not actually possess.
But the cross destroys the illusion that Jesus can be Lord of your eternity while money remains lord of your present life.
This is why ten percent can still be useful.
For many Christians, a tithe can function as a wise starting discipline—a practical benchmark for intentional generosity.
But a benchmark is not the Savior.
And ten percent must never become a weapon for condemnation where the New Testament does not explicitly impose it as the covenant law of Christ.
Some believers may prayerfully give ten percent.
Some may presently be able to give less while growing in generosity and faithfully caring for genuine obligations.
Others whom God has prospered may discover that ten percent is far below what they can joyfully give.
Think about that last possibility.
What if the danger for some Christians isn't that ten percent is too high?
What if it is too low?
Suppose God entrusts someone with extraordinary resources, yet that person says, “I gave my ten percent. The rest is mine.”
Has the Gospel really taught us to think that way?
The New Testament pushes deeper.
In 1 Corinthians 16:2, believers are instructed to set something aside in keeping with their prosperity.

In 2 Corinthians 8, Paul points to believers whose generosity emerged even amid affliction and poverty, and then reaches the Christ-centered foundation of Christian generosity: Jesus Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake so that through His poverty we might become rich—not a promise of luxury, but the staggering grace of Christ's self-giving work.
In Acts, generosity sometimes became radically sacrificial.

And yet Acts 5:4 shows that property remained under the owner's control before it was voluntarily given. The early church's generosity was remarkable precisely because it was genuine generosity—not confiscation disguised as worship.

Paul also teaches that Gospel ministry may legitimately receive material support. In 1 Corinthians 9:14, he says that the Lord directed that those proclaiming the Gospel should receive their living from the Gospel.
So yes, supporting faithful Gospel work is biblical.
Helping the poor is biblical.
Supporting those who labor in teaching and ministry is biblical.
Generous Christian giving is biblical.
But manipulating frightened Christians with promises that sending money guarantees health, wealth, or supernatural financial multiplication is another matter entirely.
Please hear this carefully.
You cannot buy God's love.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot donate enough money to erase your sin.
Your offering cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus can.
The scandal at the center of Christianity is that bankrupt sinners cannot pay their debt.
Christ paid it.
We did not climb to God with offerings.
God came down to us in Christ.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Forgiveness is received through faith in Christ, not purchased through religious transactions.
And once grace captures a person...
something happens to the hands.
They begin opening.
Not because a preacher frightened them.
Not because an algorithm pressured them.
Not because somebody promised them a mansion if they sent money.
Because the heart has encountered a Savior who gave everything necessary to rescue sinners.
That changes giving.
Perhaps that is the question you needed more than, “Do I still have to tithe?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
Has Jesus reached my wallet because Jesus has reached my heart?
Be honest.
If your giving disappeared tomorrow, would anything in the Kingdom of God notice?
Do you instinctively spend on yourself and give God whatever survives?
Do you call yourself generous because you occasionally give what you never would have missed?
Or perhaps your wound is completely different.
Maybe churches have hurt you.
Maybe someone used Malachi to frighten you.
Maybe you were pressured to give money you needed for food or medicine.
Maybe spiritual authority became financial manipulation, and now every conversation about giving makes something inside you tense.
If that is your story, do not confuse Jesus with people who misused His name.
Christ does not need manipulation to produce generosity.
The Gospel creates something stronger than coercion.
Love.
Repentance.
Gratitude.
Freedom.
So, is tithing still required today?

If by “tithing” we mean that every Christian under the new covenant is explicitly commanded to give exactly ten percent under the Mosaic tithing legislation, the New Testament does not clearly establish such a universal command.
But if someone uses that conclusion to argue that Christians therefore have little responsibility to give, that conclusion runs headfirst into the New Testament.
Christian giving is not less serious under grace.
It goes deeper.
The New Testament moves the conversation from merely calculating a percentage toward a transformed heart characterized by willing, proportionate, sacrificial, cheerful generosity.
Ten percent may be a healthy beginning.
It makes a terrible finish line if God has enabled you to do far more.
And this is where Gospel Warrior must also practice what this article teaches.

If you genuinely want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting and sharing sound Christian teaching should become part of your generosity. Scripture connects generosity with thanksgiving and glory to God, but that must remain willing worship rather than spiritual pressure.
But don't stop at money.
Sometimes the offering God places in your hand is influence.
Not to make us famous.
Make Jesus known.
And don't disappear silently after reading this.
And if God has taught you a testimony about generosity that could strengthen someone else, tell it. Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Because maybe the greatest danger was never giving nine percent instead of ten.
Maybe the greatest danger was spending your whole life asking how much Jesus requires while forgetting how much Jesus gave.
At the cross, grace did not calculate the minimum.
Grace poured itself out.
So don't give because you're terrified God will stop loving you.
Give because in Christ you have discovered a love money could never purchase.
Don't give to purchase blessing.
Give because Christ Himself is your treasure.
Don't give to become redeemed.
Give because the redeemed heart is learning to hold earthly things with open hands.
And when you fail—even here—return to Jesus.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Get up.
Begin again.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of perfect people paying God enough to keep Him happy.
It is the story of sinners who could never pay their debt being rescued by a Savior who paid it completely.
And when that truth finally travels from your theology into your heart, the question begins changing.
Not merely:
“How much do I have to give?”
But:
“Jesus... after everything You have given for me, how can everything I am become worship?”
The Gospel does not merely change what leaves your hand—it changes who sits on the throne of your heart.
